title: Ensembles: Bagging, Random Forests and Boosting
description: Combining many weak or unstable models into one strong model, by averaging them (bagging) or by building them in sequence (boosting).
overview: A committee often decides better than any member. In machine learning, an ensemble combines many models so that their errors partly cancel. Two strategies dominate. Bagging trains many deep, unstable models on resampled data and averages them, which reduces variance. Boosting trains many shallow models one after another, each correcting its predecessors, which reduces bias.
Random forests (bagging with an extra decorrelating trick) and gradient-boosted trees are the strongest general-purpose methods for tabular data, and they are the usual winners of such competitions.
objectives: Derive the variance of an average of correlated predictors and explain why decorrelation matters.
Describe bootstrap aggregation and compute the out-of-bag fraction.
Explain how random forests decorrelate trees and how to tune them.
Run AdaBoost by hand and state its training error bound.
Explain gradient boosting as gradient descent in function space and compute a boosting step for squared loss.

sections.title: Why averaging helps
body: Ask 100 people to guess the number of beans in a jar. Each guess is wild, but the average of the guesses is usually close, because the individual errors point in different directions and cancel. That works only if the guessers are independent. If everybody copies the first person's answer, the average is no better than one guess. An ensemble of models works the same way, and the formula below makes the dependence on the correlation between members exact.
Suppose B predictors each have prediction variance σ² at a point x, and any two are correlated with coefficient ρ. The variance of their average is

The second term vanishes as B grows, but the first does not. The benefit of averaging is limited by the correlation between the members. If they were independent (ρ = 0) the variance would fall as 1/B. If they were identical (ρ = 1) averaging would gain nothing.

body.caption: Variance of an average of B predictors with σ² = 1. Correlation sets a floor ρσ² that more models cannot remove.

example.title: A floor on the variance
example.problem: Predictors have variance σ² = 1 and pairwise correlation ρ = 0.3. Find the variance of an average of B = 10 and of B = 100 predictors.
example.solution: B = 10: 0.3 + 0.7/10 = 0.37. B = 100: 0.3 + 0.7/100 = 0.307. Ten times as many models cut the variance by only 17%, because the correlated part remains.

body: Averaging does not change the bias of the individual models. So the best candidates to average are low-bias, high-variance models, such as deep decision trees. Ensembling also helps only if the members make different errors.

check.q: For an average of many identically distributed predictors with correlation ρ and variance σ², the variance approaches
check.a: ρσ² as the number of models grows
wrong: σ²
σ²/ρ

sections.title: Bagging
body: To average models that differ, we would like many different training sets, but we have only one. We cannot draw new training sets from the population, but the **bootstrap** imitates it: draw m examples //with replacement// from the training set. "With replacement" means each draw puts the example back, so the same example can appear twice. For a training set {a, b, c, d, e}, one bootstrap sample might be {b, b, d, e, e}: it has the same size, some examples repeated and some (a and c) missing.
**Bagging** (bootstrap aggregating, Breiman 1996) trains one model on each of B bootstrap samples and averages their predictions (for regression) or takes a majority vote (for classification):

A bootstrap sample omits some examples. The probability that a given example is missing from a sample of size m is (1 − 1/m)^m, which tends to 1/e = 0.368. So each sample contains about 63.2% of the distinct examples; for m = 10 the omitted fraction is 0.9¹⁰ = 0.349.

body.key: The omitted examples give a free validation set. For each training example, average the predictions of only the models that did not see it. The resulting out-of-bag (OOB) error estimates the test error without a separate validation split or cross-validation.

body: Bagging is most effective for unstable procedures such as deep trees, where a small change in the data changes the model a lot. For stable procedures such as linear regression or k-NN with large k it gives little gain. It never hurts bias noticeably, it parallelizes trivially, and adding more models does not cause overfitting (the variance floor of the previous section is reached and stays).

sections.title: Random forests
body: Trees grown on bootstrap samples of the same data are still strongly correlated: if one feature is very predictive, every tree splits on it near the root. By the formula above, this correlation limits the gain. A **random forest** decorrelates the trees by a second randomization: at each split, consider only a random subset of m_{try} of the n features and choose the best split among them.

list: Typical defaults are m_{try} ≈ √n for classification (10 of 100 features) and n/3 for regression.
Grow each tree deep, with little or no pruning: low bias, high variance, then rely on averaging.
Use a few hundred trees. More trees never hurt accuracy; they only cost time.
The out-of-bag error provides a built-in estimate of test error, and features can be ranked by **permutation importance**: the increase in OOB error when a feature's values are shuffled.

body: Small m_{try} gives less correlated trees (lower ρ) but weaker individual trees (higher bias). It is the main tuning parameter, along with the minimum leaf size.

body.tip: A random forest with default settings is a strong first model on tabular data. It needs no feature scaling, handles mixed types, resists overfitting, and gives feature importances.

list: Predictions cannot extrapolate beyond the range of training targets, because they are averages of training labels.
Large forests are slow and memory-hungry to store and evaluate compared with a linear model.
A forest is not interpretable the way one tree is, although importance measures and partial dependence plots help.

check.q: What does feature subsampling at each split accomplish?
check.a: It reduces the correlation between trees
wrong: It reduces the bias of each tree
It removes the need for bootstrap samples
It guarantees the trees are pruned

sections.title: Boosting and AdaBoost
body: Bagging trains its models independently and averages them. Boosting takes the opposite approach, like a student who takes a practice test, studies only the questions they missed, takes another test weighted toward those, and repeats. **Boosting** builds an ensemble sequentially. Each new model concentrates on the examples that the current ensemble gets wrong. A **weak learner** is any model slightly better than guessing; boosting turns weak learners into a strong one, often with decision stumps (one-split trees) as the learners.
**AdaBoost** (adaptive boosting, Freund and Schapire) for labels y ∈ {−1, +1}:

list: For t = 1, …, T: fit a weak learner h_t to the weighted data. Compute its weighted error ε_t = Σ w_i 1[h_t(x_i) ≠ y_i]. Set the vote weight α_t = ½ ln((1 − ε_t)/ε_t).
Update w_i ← w_i exp(−α_t y_i h_t(x_i)) and normalize to sum 1. Misclassified examples gain weight and correct ones lose it.
Output H(x) = sign( Σ_t α_t h_t(x) ).

body: A learner with ε_t = 0.5 (no better than chance) gets weight α_t = 0, and one with lower error gets a larger weight.

example.title: One round of AdaBoost
example.problem: There are five examples with equal weights 0.2. The first weak learner misclassifies exactly one of them. Compute α₁ and the new weights.
solution: The misclassified example's weight is multiplied by e^{0.693} = 2 and becomes 0.4. Each of the four correct examples is multiplied by e^{−0.693} = 0.5 and becomes 0.1. The sum is 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8.

After normalizing, the misclassified example has weight 0.4/0.8 = 0.5, and each correct example has 0.1/0.8 = 0.125. The hard example now carries half the total weight, so the next learner must get it right.

body: AdaBoost minimizes the **exponential loss** Σ exp(−y_i F(x_i)) of the additive model F = Σ α_t h_t by stagewise optimization. The normalizer in each round is Z_t = 2√(ε_t(1 − ε_t)), and the training error is bounded by the product ΠZ_t. In the example above Z₁ = 2√0.16 = 0.8. If each round has ε_t = 0.2, then after T rounds the training error is at most 0.8^T, which is 0.107 after T = 10 and 0.011 after T = 20. In general it falls exponentially, as exp(−2Σγ_t²) with edge γ_t = ½ − ε_t.

Boosting drives down bias by adding capacity round after round. Unlike bagging, it can overfit if run too long on noisy labels, because the exponential loss puts large weight on mislabeled points. Use shallow learners, limit the rounds, and tune on validation data.

sections.title: Gradient boosting
body: Gradient boosting generalizes AdaBoost to any differentiable loss ℓ. Think of the model F(x) as the unknown function and minimize the total loss L(F) = Σ ℓ(y_i, F(x_i)) by gradient descent in function space. The negative gradient at each training point,

gives the direction in which each prediction should move. A tree h_t is fit to these **pseudo-residuals**, so that it approximates the gradient across the whole input space, and the model takes a step: F_t = F_{t−1} + ν h_t, where ν ∈ (0, 1] is the **learning rate** (shrinkage).

list: **Squared loss**: ℓ = ½(y − F)², so r_i = y_i − F(x_i): each tree fits the ordinary residuals.
**Logistic loss**: r_i = y_i − σ(F(x_i)), the probability error (see Logistic Regression), with F the log-odds.
**Absolute loss** and **Huber loss** give robust regression; ranking losses give learning to rank.

example.title: Two boosting steps with squared loss
example.problem: Targets are y = (1, 3, 8). Start with F₀ = mean(y). A tree of one split separates the first two points from the third. Use ν = 0.5 and compute F₁, and the mean squared error before and after.
solution: F₀ = 4 for all points, with residuals (−3, −1, 4) and MSE = (9 + 1 + 16)/3 = 8.67.
The tree predicts the mean residual in each group: −2 for the first two points and 4 for the third. With ν = 0.5 the model moves half-way: F₁ = (4 − 1, 4 − 1, 4 + 2) = (3, 3, 6).
New residuals are (−2, 0, 2), so MSE = (4 + 0 + 4)/3 = 2.67. The next tree would fit these.

list: **Learning rate** ν: small values (0.01 to 0.1) need more trees but generalize much better than ν = 1.
**Number of trees**: choose by early stopping on a validation set, since boosting overfits if run too long.
**Tree depth**: shallow trees (depth 3 to 8) capture low-order interactions; a depth-1 stump gives an additive model.
**Subsampling** rows (stochastic gradient boosting) and columns per tree, and penalties on leaf values (L2 and a minimum gain), as in XGBoost and LightGBM.

body: XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost implement this method with second-order (Newton) steps that use the Hessian of the loss, histogram-based split finding, native handling of missing values and categorical features, and parallelism. They are the default choice for structured data when the best accuracy is needed.

body: **Stacking** combines models of different kinds (a forest, a neural network, a linear model). A meta-model takes their predictions as inputs and learns how much to trust each one. To avoid overfitting, the meta-model must be trained on out-of-fold predictions: each base model predicts examples it did not train on, through cross-validation. A simple average or weighted average (blending) is often almost as good.

body.tip: Ensembling helps most when the members are individually good and diverse. An average of five similar gradient-boosting models gains little. A boosted tree model and a neural network on the same data usually gain more.

body: The price of an ensemble is cost and complexity: more memory, slower prediction, and a loss of interpretability. For deployment, one may compress an ensemble into a single smaller model (distillation) by training the small model to imitate the ensemble's outputs.

check.q: Why must a stacking meta-model be trained on out-of-fold predictions?
check.a: Predictions on a base model's own training data are over-optimistic, so the meta-model would trust the wrong models
wrong: Out-of-fold predictions are always more accurate
It reduces the number of base models
The meta-model cannot use the labels otherwise

quiz.q: Three predictors each have variance 9 at a point and pairwise correlation 0.5. What is the variance of their average?
quiz.why: ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B = 4.5 + 0.5(9)/3 = 4.5 + 1.5 = 6. Dividing σ² by B alone would give 3, which is correct only for independent predictors.

quiz.q: Why does bagging a linear regression model give little improvement?
quiz.a: Resampling barely changes the fitted line, so the bagged models are almost identical and highly correlated
wrong: Bagging raises the bias of a linear model enough to cancel the variance it removes
A linear regression cannot be fit to a bootstrap sample
Linear regression already has the lowest variance of any model
quiz.why: Averaging helps only when members differ. A stable procedure gives nearly the same model on every resample, so ρ is close to 1 and the variance barely falls.

quiz.q: A bootstrap sample of 5 examples is drawn with replacement from a set of 5. What is the probability that one particular example is absent from it?
quiz.why: Each draw misses the example with probability 4/5, so the chance of missing it in 5 draws is 0.8⁵ = 0.328. The value 0.37 is the limit as m grows.

quiz.q: A bagged ensemble has σ² = 1 and ρ = 0.3 among its trees. Growing it from 100 trees to 1000 trees changes the variance of the average from 0.307 to about
quiz.why: The variance is 0.3 + 0.7/1000 = 0.3007. The floor ρσ² = 0.3 cannot be removed by adding trees, and extra trees do not cause overfitting.

quiz.q: A random forest regressor is trained on 90 features. What is the usual default number of features considered at each split?
quiz.why: The regression default is about n/3 = 30. The value 9 is √90, the default for classification.

quiz.q: Every tree in a forest splits on the same dominant feature at its root, so the trees look alike. Which change most directly lowers their correlation?
quiz.a: Lower m_try, so that the dominant feature is often unavailable at a split
wrong: Raise m_try to the full number of features
Add several hundred more trees
Prune each tree back to a few leaves
quiz.why: Restricting the candidate features forces different trees to use different splits. More trees do not change the correlation between trees, and pruning raises bias.

quiz.q: A random forest regressor is trained on house prices that range from 100k to 900k. What is the largest price it can output?
wrong: No upper limit, because trees extrapolate along trends
About 1.3 million, from the largest tree's trend
Only the average of the training prices
quiz.why: Each leaf predicts a mean of training targets, and a forest averages leaves, so every prediction lies within the range of the training labels.

quiz.q: The permutation importance of a feature in a random forest is
quiz.a: the increase in out-of-bag error after the feature's values are shuffled
wrong: the total impurity decrease from splits on the feature
the number of trees that use the feature at the root
the correlation between the feature and the target
quiz.why: Shuffling a useful feature breaks its link to the target, so the error rises. Total impurity decrease is the other, less reliable, importance measure.

quiz.q: In AdaBoost, a weak learner has weighted error 0.25. What is its vote weight α?
quiz.why: α = ½ ln(0.75/0.25) = ½ ln 3 = 0.549. Omitting the ½ gives 1.10, and inverting the ratio gives −0.55.

quiz.q: Four examples start with weight 0.25 each in AdaBoost, and the learner misclassifies one of them. After the update and normalization, what is the weight of the misclassified example?
quiz.why: With ε = 0.25, α = 0.549, the wrong example's weight is multiplied by √3, to 0.433, and each correct one by 1/√3, to 0.144. The total is 0.866, so the wrong example holds 0.433/0.866 = 0.5.

quiz.q: Every round of AdaBoost has weighted error 0.1. What is the bound on the training error after 3 rounds?
quiz.why: Each round's normalizer is Z = 2√(0.1 · 0.9) = 0.6, and the bound is the product Z³ = 0.216. Cubing the error 0.1 would ignore the factor of 2√(ε(1 − ε)).

quiz.q: A dataset has 10% of its labels flipped at random. Which method is likely to cope better, and why?
quiz.a: A random forest, because AdaBoost's exponential loss puts large weight on the mislabeled points
wrong: AdaBoost, because it focuses on the examples that are hardest to classify
They cope equally, since every ensemble averages out label noise
Neither can cope, since ensembles need perfectly labeled data
quiz.why: Boosting keeps increasing the weight of examples it misclassifies, and flipped labels are exactly those. A forest averages independent deep trees, which dilutes the effect of noise.

quiz.q: Squared-loss gradient boosting has targets y = (2, 4, 12) and F₀ = the mean. A tree fits the residuals exactly and ν = 0.5. What is F₁ at the third point?
quiz.why: F₀ = 6, so the third residual is 6, and F₁ = 6 + 0.5(6) = 9. With ν = 1 the model would jump to 12, and 3 is the step alone without the starting value.

quiz.q: In gradient boosting with logistic loss and labels coded 0 and 1, a point has y = 1 and current log-odds F(x) = 0. What is its pseudo-residual?
quiz.why: The residual is y − σ(F) = 1 − σ(0) = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5. The log-odds of 0 mean the model predicts probability 0.5.

quiz.q: Gradient boosting uses depth-1 trees (stumps) as its base learners. The resulting model is
quiz.a: additive in the features, with no interactions between them
wrong: linear in the features
a model with all pairwise interactions
equivalent to a single decision tree
quiz.why: Each stump depends on one feature, so the sum is a sum of one-variable functions. These functions are piecewise constant, so the model is additive but not linear.

quiz.q: Why is gradient boosting described as gradient descent in function space?
quiz.a: Each new tree approximates the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, and the model steps along it
wrong: The weights of every earlier tree are adjusted by backpropagation
The learning rate is decreased along the gradient of the features
Each tree is fit to the gradient of the loss with respect to the inputs x
quiz.why: The model's predictions at the training points are the variable being optimized. The pseudo-residuals give the direction, and a tree generalizes that direction to unseen inputs.

quiz.q: Which pair of models is likely to gain most from being combined in an ensemble?
quiz.a: A gradient-boosted tree model and a neural network trained on the same data
wrong: Five boosted tree models trained with the same settings and different seeds
Two random forests with 400 and 500 trees on the same data
A gradient-boosted model and a copy of it with a different learning rate
quiz.why: Ensembling pays off when members are individually good and make different errors. Models of different families differ more than near copies of the same model.

summary: The variance of an average of correlated predictors is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B. Averaging reduces variance but leaves the bias, and correlation sets a floor.
Bagging averages models trained on bootstrap samples. Each sample leaves out about 36.8% of the data, which gives the out-of-bag error estimate for free.
Random forests add random feature subsets at each split to decorrelate the trees. They are robust and need little tuning.
AdaBoost reweights examples and weights learners by α = ½ ln((1 − ε)/ε); its training error falls exponentially. Boosting reduces bias but can overfit noise.
Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss (the residuals for squared loss) and steps with a small learning rate. XGBoost-style implementations dominate tabular tasks.
Stacking and blending combine different model families when their errors differ.

problems.q: An ensemble of B = 25 predictors has σ² = 4 and correlation ρ = 0.2. Compute the variance of the average.
problems.a: 0.928, compared with 4 for a single predictor.

problems.q: A forest is built from 200 bootstrap samples of a data set with m = 1000 examples. About how many trees leave out a specific example, on average?
problems.solution: Each tree omits the example with probability (1 − 1/1000)^{1000} ≈ 0.368. Expected number of trees: 200 × 0.368 ≈ 74.
problems.a: About 74 trees, which are used for its out-of-bag prediction.

problems.q: In AdaBoost, a weak learner has weighted error 0.1. Compute α, and the factor by which misclassified and correctly classified weights are multiplied before normalization.

Gradient boosting with squared loss and ν = 0.1 starts with F₀ = 10 at a point whose target is y = 16. The first tree predicts the residual exactly. Compute F₁, and the number of trees needed before the error at this point falls below 0.1, assuming each tree fits the current residual exactly.
problems.solution: The residual is 6, and F₁ = 10 + 0.1(6) = 10.6, leaving residual 5.4. Each tree shrinks the residual by the factor 0.9, so after t trees it is 6(0.9)^t. Setting 6(0.9)^t < 0.1 gives t > ln(60)/(−ln 0.9) = 4.094/0.1054 = 38.9.

problems.q: A random forest on data with n = 64 features uses m_{try} = √n. How many features are considered at each split, and what happens to tree correlation if m_{try} is raised to 64?
problems.solution: √64 = 8 features per split. With m_{try} = 64 every split considers all features, so trees depend only on the bootstrap sampling and become more correlated, which reduces the gain from averaging (the method becomes plain bagging).
problems.a: 8 features; the forest becomes ordinary bagging with more correlated trees.
